name: Financial Times cryptic crossword, Penguin book 1 No 5

book.title: The Penguin Book of Financial Times Crosswords, volume 1

clue.text: Restrain the companion round the river

indicators.note: one thing set round another wraps it, so the companion word encloses the river word

blocks.note: a mate is a companion
the Oder is a river of central Europe

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hold back a friend who is wandering about near a river.
explanation.walkthrough: MATE is split so that the Oder sits inside it: M-ODER-ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate something is to temper or hold it in check, a plain verb synonym.

clue.text: She's after me with her toils

indicators.note: after says the first piece comes later in the answer than the second piece

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A woman follows the speaker about, burdened with all her labours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toils' looks like hard work; it is the noun meaning nets or snares, as in 'caught in the toils'.
explanation.definitionFit: Toils in the older sense are nets used to trap game, and meshes are also nets or entanglements.

clue.text: Scoop for a nervy doctor

blocks.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
someone nervy is on edge

explanation.surface: A journalist's scoop is about a jittery physician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoop' suggests a news story; it is the verb for digging up mud from a riverbed.
explanation.definitionFit: To dredge is to scoop silt or objects up from the bottom of water, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Concerning the man in the street in London

definitions.note: the answer names the street, Regent Street

blocks.note: re means concerning or regarding
a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: Something has to do with the ordinary Londoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The man in the street' looks like the average person, but the phrase is split: 'the man' is wordplay and 'the street in London' is Regent Street, a major West End shopping street.
explanation.definitionFit: Regent Street is one of central London's best-known shopping thoroughfares, named after the Prince Regent.

clue.text: Lost the argument like an aircraft coming in

blocks.note: first meaning: was out-argued, silenced by someone else's talk
second meaning: a plane guided to land by radio instructions from the ground

explanation.walkthrough: Air traffic controllers can guide a pilot to land by radio, step by step, which is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To be out-talked is to lose a debate, and a plane landed with spoken directions from controllers has the same phrase applied to it.

clue.text: Experts show flaws

blocks.note: first meaning: crack shots or crack players, people who are top of their field
second meaning: splits or faults in a surface

explanation.surface: Specialists reveal the weaknesses in something.
explanation.walkthrough: As a noun, a 'crack' is an expert, mostly in older or informal British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracks are fissures or defects, and in informal usage a crack is also a highly skilled person, so the plural serves both.

clue.text: Withdraws the sappers round the region

indicators.note: something put round another encloses it, so the sappers are split either side of the region

blocks.note: sappers are soldiers of the Royal Engineers, RE, made plural
a tract is an area or region of land

explanation.surface: Army engineers pull back from around a territory.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper is the name for a Royal Engineers soldier, so several of them are taken as REs, which wraps the region.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract is to draw back or take back, so withdraws is a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: 'How nature always does — ' (Iolanthe)

blocks.note: surface reading: an unfinished remark about how nature behaves
setter's reading: fill the gap from Private Willis's song in Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera

explanation.walkthrough: The song runs 'I often think it's comical how Nature always does contrive that every boy and every gal that's born into the world alive is either a little Liberal or else a little Conservative.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb in Gilbert's lyric is the one meaning to devise or bring about by skill.

clue.text: The innocent are not so much after a little drink

definitions.note: adjective; the clue phrases it as a noun

indicators.note: after places the first-named piece later in the answer than the second

blocks.note: a spot is a small amount of drink
less means a smaller amount

explanation.surface: Innocent people drink less than others.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotless means without moral stain, blameless, which is what being innocent comes to.

clue.text: Villain in a novel hat

blocks.note: surface reading: a bad guy in some new kind of headgear
setter's reading: one title that names both a book and a soft felt hat, Du Maurier's Trilby

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer sports an unusual new hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new', but it is a book: George du Maurier's Trilby (1894), whose title is also the name of a hat. Its villain is the hypnotist Svengali.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali is the sinister hypnotist who controls the heroine in du Maurier's book, and his name now means any manipulative controlling figure.

clue.text: Drink for the smart circle

blocks.note: to smart is to sting with pain
the letter O is round like a circle

explanation.surface: A cocktail is suited to a fashionable social set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart circle' looks like a fashionable set of people; 'smart' is the verb meaning to hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingo is an old name for strong ale or beer, so it is a kind of alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: The R.E. at length means to 7

blocks.note: first meaning: R.E. written out in full is the Royal ..., whose members are soldiers of that trade
second meaning: a verb for bringing something about, the sense of the answer to 7 down

explanation.surface: Religious Education, discussed at length, is the way to devise something.
explanation.walkthrough: R.E. could be the school subject, but 'at length' means spelt out: Royal Engineers. 7 down is CONTRIVE, and to engineer a result is to contrive it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapper of the Royal Engineers is a military engineer, and to engineer a plan is to contrive or arrange it cleverly.

clue.text: This man is on the beat in the U.S.A.

definitions.text: This man is on the beat in the U.S.A.

blocks.clueFragment: This man is on the beat in the U.S.A.
blocks.note: surface reading: an American police officer walking his regular route
setter's reading: the light followed by the word 'man' names that American officer

explanation.surface: An American police officer walks his regular route.
explanation.walkthrough: An American beat cop is a patrolman; the answer is the light plus 'man', which is what 'This man' points at.
explanation.definitionFit: A patrol is the round of a beat, and the American word for a beat officer adds man to it.

clue.text: Cleaners that put chaps off

blocks.note: with the final word of the clue, to put off is to discourage
gents are men, chaps
the second half of the phrasal verb begun two words earlier

explanation.surface: Some cleaning women discourage male admirers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put chaps off' is read with the verb wrapped round its object, so the putting-off piece comes first and the chaps follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Detergents are cleaning agents such as washing powder, so they are cleaners.

clue.text: They express qualities that make cadets jive

indicators.note: to make something out of material is to build it anew, so the following letters are rebuilt into a different word

blocks.note: the two words are taken as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Something gives young officer trainees the qualities to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jive' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjectives are the parts of speech that describe attributes of nouns, such as big, red or kind.

clue.text: Once a flier but has now gone off the rails

definitions.text: Once a flier but has now gone off the rails

blocks.clueFragment: Once a flier but has now gone off the rails
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who was once a success has since gone astray
setter's reading: the famous London to Edinburgh steam locomotive, called Flying, has been retired from service

explanation.walkthrough: The Flying Scotsman is a celebrated British steam locomotive on the London to Edinburgh route; by the time of this puzzle it was out of regular service. 'Off the rails' looks like 'gone wild'.
explanation.definitionFit: The locomotive's name drops its first word to leave a man from Scotland, and being withdrawn it no longer runs on the main line.

clue.text: Fresh hops served at intervals

blocks.note: fresh means new
a hop is an informal dance, as a ball is a formal one

explanation.surface: Freshly picked hops are brought out every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis the umpire calls for new balls after a set number of games, so they come into service at intervals.
explanation.definitionFit: In a tennis match fresh balls are brought into play after a fixed run of games, so they are served periodically.

clue.text: Meant to be a bride some day

definitions.text: to be a bride some day

blocks.note: first meaning: planned or designed, as in deliberate

blocks.clueFragment: to be a bride some day
blocks.note: second meaning: a fiancée, someone's future wife

explanation.walkthrough: As a noun the word is an old-fashioned name for the person one is engaged to.
explanation.definitionFit: Something intended was planned or deliberate, and one's intended is a betrothed partner who will marry later.

clue.text: A pure lottery but it's revolutionary to make it

definitions.note: describes the answer rather than naming it

blocks.note: pure means unsullied, spotless
a sweepstake, a draw in which the pooled stakes go to the winners

explanation.surface: A raffle is pure chance, yet winning it would change your life.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: to make a clean sweep is to remove everything old at once, which is a revolutionary act.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a clean sweep means a complete change, getting rid of all existing people or things, so the idiom is revolution in miniature.

clue.text: A blow the cox must face

blocks.note: first meaning: a hit or knock
second meaning: the rower who sits nearest the stern, facing the coxswain and setting the pace

explanation.surface: The coxswain of a boat must take a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a rowing eight the stroke sits facing the cox, who steers from the stern.
explanation.definitionFit: A stroke is a hit, and in rowing it is also the oarsman whose seat faces the cox and sets the rhythm.

clue.text: Cuts the wood in a ship

indicators.note: in means placed within, so the wood sits inside the ship

blocks.note: teak is a hard wood used in boatbuilding
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Someone saws up the timber on board a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuts' looks like a verb about sawing; it is a noun for pieces of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Steaks are thick slices of beef or fish, so they are cuts from a butcher.

clue.text: A form of debris we have heard of in the bath (©)

definitions.text: we have heard of in the bath

indicators.note: a form of something is a different shape of it, so these letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Some rubbish is rumoured to have turned up in the bathtub.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Brides in the Bath' case of 1915 was a notorious British murder trial: George Joseph Smith drowned three wives in their baths.
explanation.definitionFit: The women killed by George Joseph Smith became known to the press as the Brides in the Bath, a phrase still familiar in Britain.

clue.text: The pad is leased to a Cambridge man

blocks.note: short for Cantab, a member of Cambridge University
property that is let is leased out

explanation.surface: A flat is rented out to a Cambridge student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pad' suggests a flat to live in, matching 'leased'; here it is a writing pad. The leased part is added to the Cambridge man.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet is a pad of writing paper fastened at one edge, as in a notepaper block.

clue.text: Found at Speakers' Corner or in the launderette

blocks.note: first meaning: a rabble-rousing orator stirring up a crowd
second meaning: the paddle in a washing machine that churns the clothes

explanation.surface: Something can be seen either at a famous spot for public speeches or at a coin laundry.
explanation.walkthrough: Speakers' Corner is a spot in London's Hyde Park where anyone may stand up and harangue passers-by; a launderette is a coin-operated laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses stir things up: a political rabble-rouser stirs a crowd, and the central spindle of a washer stirs the laundry.

clue.text: Sickness keeps the boy inside a month

indicators.note: inside places one item within the other, so the boy goes within the month

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
May is a month of the year

explanation.surface: An illness keeps a boy indoors for a whole month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inside' looks like 'indoors'; it puts the boy within May.
explanation.definitionFit: A malady is an illness or disease, an old-fashioned noun synonym.

clue.text: To a room in the hospital — how inconvenient

blocks.note: un is the French word for a
taken as written
a ward is a room for patients in a hospital

explanation.surface: Being sent to a hospital ward is a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is uncertain: reading the article as French is a guess, and the clue gives the words in a different order from the answer. The setter may simply mean 'not to a ward'.
explanation.definitionFit: Untoward means unfortunate, awkward or unseemly, so an untoward event is an inconvenient one.

clue.text: Don't put on airs — the game is over

blocks.note: first meaning: putting on side is showing off, so this is an order against swank
second meaning: the referee's call that ends a rugby match

explanation.surface: Stop showing off, the match has finished.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'side' means conceit, so 'no side!' means stop putting on airs. In rugby the referee calls 'no side' when the match ends.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the rugby term for full time and a ban on swagger or haughtiness.

clue.text: Values — the jennies?

blocks.note: first meaning: works out the worth of something, as an appraiser does
second meaning, whimsical: female donkeys, read as an ass with the feminine ending -ess, made plural

explanation.walkthrough: A jenny is a female donkey. On the model of lioness, a female ass would be an 'ass-ess', and the question mark flags this made-up plural.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to judge the worth of property or work, a direct verb synonym for values.
